items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we introduce a method of integration that can be used in cases where integration by substitution fails. The method is known as integration by parts. The so-called by-parts formula is

Content:
[MATH: \int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
or simply

Content:
[MATH: \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
This method is handy for integrating products of functions where one factor can be easily integrated, and the other factor can easily be differentiated.

Content:
Let's see how to apply it to evaluate the integral

Content:
[MATH: \int xe^{2x} \textrm{d}x\,.]

Content:
The idea is to call one of the factors [MATH: u,] the other factor [MATH: v',] and then apply the by-parts formula. We'll choose the following:

Content:
[MATH: \int \underbrace{\color{blue}x}_{\large\color{blue}u}\cdot \underbrace{\color{red}e^{2x}}_{\large\color{red}v'} \textrm{d}x]

Content:
Now, if [MATH: {\color{blue}u} = {\color{blue}x}] then we differentiate to get [MATH: {\color{blue}u'} = {\color{blue}1}.] And if [MATH: {\color{red}v'} = {\color{red}e^{2x}}] then we integrate to get [MATH: {\color{red}v} = {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}}.] Note that we don't bother with the constant of integration here.

Content:
We now have everything we need, so we can substitute into the "by-parts" formula, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∫x ⋅ e^{2x}_(⏟)_(uv^{′})dx|= x ⋅ (1)/(2)e^{2x}_(⏟)_(uv) − ∫(1)/(2)e^{2x} ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(vu^{′})dx]

Content:
Now, we compute the integral:

Content:
[MATH: ∫xe^{2x}dx|= (1)/(2)xe^{2x} − (1)/(2)∫e^{2x}dx; = (1)/(2)xe^{2x} − (1)/(2) ⋅ (1)/(2)e^{2x} + C; = (1)/(2)xe^{2x} − (1)/(4)e^{2x} + C; = (1)/(4)e^{2x}(2x − 1) + C]

Content:
And we're done! Notice that integration by parts allows us to take a complicated integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{2x}\,\textrm{d}x] and replace it with the simpler [MATH: \displaystyle \int e^{2x}\,\textrm{d}x] plus some additional terms.

sections.normalized_html: Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{7x} \textrm{d}x.]
sections.readable_text: Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{7x} \textrm{d}x.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

[MATH: \int uv' \, \textrm{d}x= uv - \int vu' \, \textrm{d}x.]

We need to express [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{7x} \textrm{d}x] as [MATH: \displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.] Therefore, we set

[MATH: u = x|⟹u^{′} = 1; v^{′} = e^{7x}|⟹v = (1)/(7)e^{7x}.]

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get the following:

[MATH: ∫uv^{′}dx|= uv − ∫vu^{′}dx; ∫x ⋅ e^{7x}dx|= x ⋅ (1)/(7)e^{7x} − ∫(1)/(7)e^{7x} ⋅ 1dx]

Finally, we calculate the integral:

[MATH: ∫xe^{7x}dx|= (1)/(7)xe^{7x} − (1)/(7)∫e^{7x}dx; = (1)/(7)xe^{7x} − (1)/(7)((e^{7x})/(7)) + C; = (1)/(7)xe^{7x} − (1)/(49)e^{7x} + C]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:

[MATH: \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x.]

We need to express [MATH: \displaystyle \int x \cos{2x} \textrm{d}x] as [MATH: \displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.] Therefore, we set

[MATH: u = x|⟹u^{′} = 1; v^{′} = \cos 2x|⟹v = (1)/(2)\sin 2x.]

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/5} x\sin(5x) \, \textrm{d}x.]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/5} x\sin(5x) \, \textrm{d}x.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

[MATH: u = x|⟹u^{′} = 1; v^{′} = \sin (5x)|⟹v = − (1)/(5)\cos (5x).]

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

[MATH: ∫uv^{′}dx|= uv − ∫vu^{′}dx; ∫x ⋅ \sin (5x)dx|= − x ⋅ (1)/(5)\cos (5x) − ∫(− (1)/(5)\cos (5x)) ⋅ 1dx.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{π/5}x\sin (5x)dx|= − (1)/(5)x\cos (5x)|_{0}^{π/5} + (1)/(5)∫_{0}^{π/5}\cos (5x)dx; = − (1)/(5)x\cos (5x)|_{0}^{π/5} + (1)/(5)((\sin (5x))/(5))|_{0}^{π/5}; = [− (1)/(5) ⋅ (π)/(5)\cos (π) + (1)/(5) ⋅ 0 ⋅ \cos (0)] + [(1)/(25)\sin (π) − (1)/(25)\sin (0)]; = [− (π)/(25) ⋅ (− 1) + 0] + [0 − 0]; = (π)/(25).]

Content:
If you thought the by-parts formula looked similar to the product rule for differentiation, then you'd be right. In fact, that's precisely where it comes from!

Content:
To work out the formula, we recall the product rule for differentiation,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)=u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}+ v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x},]

Content:
where [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] are functions of [MATH: x.]

Content:
If we rearrange this formula a bit, we get

Content:
[MATH: u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)- v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}.]
Let's now integrate both sides of the equation:

Content:
[MATH: \int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x=\int\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)\,\textrm{d}x- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
Using the fundamental theorem of calculus, we can use the fact that [MATH: \displaystyle\int\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)\,\textrm{d}x=uv,] and we arrive at the by-parts formula:

Content:
[MATH: \int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we introduce a method of integration that can be used in cases where integration by substitution fails. The method is known as integration by parts. The so-called by-parts formula is

Content:
[MATH: \int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
or simply

Content:
[MATH: \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
This method is handy for integrating products of functions where one factor can be easily integrated, and the other factor can easily be differentiated.

Content:
Let's see how to apply it to evaluate the integral

Content:
[MATH: \int xe^{2x} \textrm{d}x\,.]

Content:
The idea is to call one of the factors [MATH: u,] the other factor [MATH: v',] and then apply the by-parts formula. We'll choose the following:

Content:
[MATH: \int \underbrace{\color{blue}x}_{\large\color{blue}u}\cdot \underbrace{\color{red}e^{2x}}_{\large\color{red}v'} \textrm{d}x]

Content:
Now, if [MATH: {\color{blue}u} = {\color{blue}x}] then we differentiate to get [MATH: {\color{blue}u'} = {\color{blue}1}.] And if [MATH: {\color{red}v'} = {\color{red}e^{2x}}] then we integrate to get [MATH: {\color{red}v} = {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}}.] Note that we don't bother with the constant of integration here.

Content:
We now have everything we need, so we can substitute into the "by-parts" formula, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∫x ⋅ e^{2x}_(⏟)_(uv^{′})dx|= x ⋅ (1)/(2)e^{2x}_(⏟)_(uv) − ∫(1)/(2)e^{2x} ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(vu^{′})dx]

Content:
Now, we compute the integral:

Content:
[MATH: ∫xe^{2x}dx|= (1)/(2)xe^{2x} − (1)/(2)∫e^{2x}dx; = (1)/(2)xe^{2x} − (1)/(2) ⋅ (1)/(2)e^{2x} + C; = (1)/(2)xe^{2x} − (1)/(4)e^{2x} + C; = (1)/(4)e^{2x}(2x − 1) + C]

Content:
And we're done! Notice that integration by parts allows us to take a complicated integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{2x}\,\textrm{d}x] and replace it with the simpler [MATH: \displaystyle \int e^{2x}\,\textrm{d}x] plus some additional terms.

Item 2 — Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing an Exponential Expression

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{7x} \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

[MATH: \int uv' \, \textrm{d}x= uv - \int vu' \, \textrm{d}x.]

We need to express [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{7x} \textrm{d}x] as [MATH: \displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.] Therefore, we set

[MATH: u = x|⟹u^{′} = 1; v^{′} = e^{7x}|⟹v = (1)/(7)e^{7x}.]

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get the following:

[MATH: ∫uv^{′}dx|= uv − ∫vu^{′}dx; ∫x ⋅ e^{7x}dx|= x ⋅ (1)/(7)e^{7x} − ∫(1)/(7)e^{7x} ⋅ 1dx]

Finally, we calculate the integral:

[MATH: ∫xe^{7x}dx|= (1)/(7)xe^{7x} − (1)/(7)∫e^{7x}dx; = (1)/(7)xe^{7x} − (1)/(7)((e^{7x})/(7)) + C; = (1)/(7)xe^{7x} − (1)/(49)e^{7x} + C]

Item 5 — Example: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle\int x \cos{2x}\,\textrm d x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

[MATH: \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x.]

We need to express [MATH: \displaystyle \int x \cos{2x} \textrm{d}x] as [MATH: \displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.] Therefore, we set

[MATH: u = x|⟹u^{′} = 1; v^{′} = \cos 2x|⟹v = (1)/(2)\sin 2x.]

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

[MATH: ∫uv^{′}dx|= uv − ∫vu^{′}dx; ∫x\cos 2xdx|= x ⋅ (1)/(2)\sin 2x − ∫(1)/(2)\sin 2x ⋅ 1dx.]

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

[MATH: ∫x\cos 2xdx|= (1)/(2)x\sin 2x − (1)/(2)∫\sin 2xdx; = (1)/(2)x\sin 2x − (1)/(2)(− (1)/(2)\cos 2x) + C; = (1)/(2)x\sin 2x + (1)/(4)\cos 2x + C]

Item 8 — Example: Computing a Definite Integral Using Integration by Parts

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/5} x\sin(5x) \, \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

[MATH: u = x|⟹u^{′} = 1; v^{′} = \sin (5x)|⟹v = − (1)/(5)\cos (5x).]

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

[MATH: ∫uv^{′}dx|= uv − ∫vu^{′}dx; ∫x ⋅ \sin (5x)dx|= − x ⋅ (1)/(5)\cos (5x) − ∫(− (1)/(5)\cos (5x)) ⋅ 1dx.]

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{π/5}x\sin (5x)dx|= − (1)/(5)x\cos (5x)|_{0}^{π/5} + (1)/(5)∫_{0}^{π/5}\cos (5x)dx; = − (1)/(5)x\cos (5x)|_{0}^{π/5} + (1)/(5)((\sin (5x))/(5))|_{0}^{π/5}; = [− (1)/(5) ⋅ (π)/(5)\cos (π) + (1)/(5) ⋅ 0 ⋅ \cos (0)] + [(1)/(25)\sin (π) − (1)/(25)\sin (0)]; = [− (π)/(25) ⋅ (− 1) + 0] + [0 − 0]; = (π)/(25).]

Item 11 — Tutorial: Deriving the By Parts Formula From the Product Rule

Content:
If you thought the by-parts formula looked similar to the product rule for differentiation, then you'd be right. In fact, that's precisely where it comes from!

Content:
To work out the formula, we recall the product rule for differentiation,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)=u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}+ v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x},]

Content:
where [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] are functions of [MATH: x.]

Content:
If we rearrange this formula a bit, we get

Content:
[MATH: u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)- v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}.]
Let's now integrate both sides of the equation:

Content:
[MATH: \int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x=\int\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)\,\textrm{d}x- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
Using the fundamental theorem of calculus, we can use the fact that [MATH: \displaystyle\int\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(uv)\,\textrm{d}x=uv,] and we arrive at the by-parts formula:

Content:
[MATH: \int u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Final Remark

Content:
Let's go back to our first example,

Content:
[MATH: \int xe^{2x} \textrm{d}x\,.]

Content:
Note that when we selected our [MATH: u] and [MATH: v',] we could have picked them the other way around. So instead, we could have said

Content:
[MATH: u = e^{2x}|⟹u^{′} = 2e^{2x}; v^{′} = x|⟹v = (1)/(2)x^{2}.]

Content:
Applying the by-parts formula using this selection, we get

Content:
[MATH: ∫xe^{2x}dx|= (1)/(2)x^{2}e^{2x} − ∫x^{2}e^{2x}dx.]

Content:
Now, while the above is a mathematically correct statement, the integral on the right-hand side is more complicated than the integral we started with. Ouch!

Content:
Therefore, it's crucial that we select our [MATH: u] and [MATH: v'] in such a way that the problem is simplified, not made more complicated.
